metadata.title: Detailed CSE Reading Material
metadata.audience: CSE graduate candidates preparing for fundamentals, interviews, and written assessments
designNotes: Unicode sketches are used only where they stay compact.
Detailed visual study is delegated to curated reference links per topic.
Content is arranged topic-wise and difficulty-tagged Easy, Medium, or Hard.
Each topic includes learning objectives, notes, formulas/rules, traps, practice drills, and references.

globalStudyPlan: Round 1: Read every Easy topic and solve small examples until definitions are automatic.
Round 2: For each Medium topic, make a handwritten invariant/formula sheet and solve mixed MCQ/MSQ/code-trace questions.
Round 3: For each Hard topic, force yourself to explain edge cases, failure modes, and calculation shortcuts aloud.
Round 4: Revisit mistakes by classifying them as concept gap, formula gap, reading-comprehension gap, or careless arithmetic.
Round 5: Simulate timed tests with interleaved subjects; real assessments rarely group topics conveniently.

referenceCatalog.bestFor: Lists, tuples, sets, dictionaries, looping idioms, and core Python container behavior.

referenceCatalog.title: Python Documentation: Built-in Types
referenceCatalog.bestFor: Truthiness, numeric operations, sequences, mappings, iterators, and string behavior.

referenceCatalog.title: Python Documentation: itertools, functools, collections

referenceCatalog.title: cppreference: C Reference
referenceCatalog.bestFor: C language syntax, standard library functions, memory allocation, undefined behavior notes.

referenceCatalog.title: cppreference: C++ Reference
referenceCatalog.bestFor: C++ value categories, references, templates, containers, algorithms, smart pointers, and standard-library details.

referenceCatalog.title: cppreference: malloc
referenceCatalog.bestFor: Precise behavior of C dynamic memory allocation and deallocation contracts.

referenceCatalog.title: Open Data Structures
referenceCatalog.bestFor: Readable implementations and analysis of lists, trees, hash tables, heaps, graphs, and advanced structures.

referenceCatalog.title: CP-Algorithms

referenceCatalog.title: MIT OpenCourseWare 6.006 Introduction to Algorithms

referenceCatalog.title: MIT OpenCourseWare 6.046J Design and Analysis of Algorithms
referenceCatalog.bestFor: Advanced algorithm design, graph algorithms, NP-completeness, approximation, and randomized algorithms.

referenceCatalog.title: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces
referenceCatalog.publisher: Remzi H. Arpaci-Dusseau and Andrea C. Arpaci-Dusseau
referenceCatalog.bestFor: Processes, scheduling, virtual memory, concurrency, file systems, and OS design intuition.

referenceCatalog.title: Linux man-pages project
referenceCatalog.bestFor: System calls, process APIs, signals, file descriptors, sockets, and POSIX/Linux behavior.

referenceCatalog.title: CMU 15-445/645 Database Systems
referenceCatalog.bestFor: DBMS internals: storage, indexing, query execution, optimization, transactions, recovery, and concurrency.

referenceCatalog.title: PostgreSQL Documentation
referenceCatalog.bestFor: Practical SQL, indexing, transactions, query planning, constraints, and database administration.

referenceCatalog.title: Use The Index, Luke!
referenceCatalog.bestFor: SQL indexing, query performance, selectivity, composite indexes, sorting, and pagination.

referenceCatalog.title: Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach Resources

referenceCatalog.bestFor: IPv6 header format, extension headers, addressing, and packet-processing rules.

referenceCatalog.title: RFC 1035: Domain Names - Implementation and Specification

referenceCatalog.publisher: Randal E. Bryant and David R. O'Hallaron
referenceCatalog.bestFor: Machine-level programming, memory hierarchy, linking, exceptional control flow, and system performance.

subjects.title: Programming Fundamentals
subjects.overview: The common mental model behind C, Python, and C++: how programs represent data, choose control paths, decompose logic, handle errors, and trade clarity against performance.

topics.title: Program decomposition and problem solving
learningObjectives: Define program decomposition and problem solving precisely and connect it to input-process-output, state, invariants.
Trace a representative example without guessing intermediate states.
State the important invariants, assumptions, and failure modes.
Solve at least one calculation, code-tracing, or design-style problem related to the topic.
coreNotes: Primary focus: input-process-output, state, invariants, edge cases. Learn these as connected rules rather than isolated definitions.
Mental model: for program decomposition and problem solving, identify the objects involved, the operation being performed, the invariant that must remain true, and the cost paid.
Separate syntax from semantics: syntax tells what is legal, semantics tells what happens.
Track state explicitly. In confusing code, write variable values after each statement.
Interview depth target (Easy): define the concept, trace a small example, explain a non-obvious edge case, and state when the common shortcut fails.
Implementation angle: write or inspect code/pseudocode for program decomposition and problem solving and annotate each line with state changes, memory effects, or resource usage where applicable.
Calculation angle: know which quantities are counted for program decomposition and problem solving—items, bytes, bits, blocks, pages, edges, tuples, cycles, packets, or clock periods.
Revision strategy: keep a one-page sheet with definitions, invariants, formulas, traps, and two solved examples for program decomposition and problem solving.
Ask which operations mutate existing objects and which create new values.
For each construct, learn the smallest rule that predicts all edge cases.
